Last week, we introduced MiniMed Flex with Simplera in Western Europe, with Flex now available in 9 European countries following a successful early customer experience phase across 5 markets. The initial interest from patients and physicians has been strong. Flex with Instinct received CE Mark last month and remains on track to launch in our fiscal fourth quarter. Together, these debuts give people more choice in pumps and sensors and give us more ways to meet the needs and preferences of people living with diabetes.

    We believe we are well positioned to launch Flex into a strong and growing Western European business with strong pump demand, more sensor options and established commercial and market access infrastructure. Our ability to commercialize at scale is an important advantage. Simplera is now available in over 50 countries and Instinct in 14, supported by our reimbursement capabilities, clinical relationships and customer support infrastructure across the region. Together, these capabilities and our expanding product portfolio give us confidence in a long runway for durable international growth. Now let me turn to our innovation pipeline. Last quarter, I told you we were not launching individual products. We were building the next generation of MiniMed, one company, every option, one ecosystem.

    Three months later, several of those programs have taken another important leap forward. More importantly, we continue to deliver on the roadmap we laid out when we separated from Medtronic with products moving from development to pivotal trials, from trials to submission to approval and from approval to commercialization. Let me start with MiniMed Fit. Earlier this month, we received FDA clearance for Fit several months ahead of expectations and just a couple of months after our submission in late August. As a result, we now expect to accelerate our early customer experience phase in Q4 this fiscal year and shift left the full U.S. commercial launch to spring of 2027. MiniMed Fit is a major strategic milestone for MiniMed.

    It brings our differentiated therapy platform to a newly introduced segment for MiniMed and the fastest-growing segment of insulin delivery. We began preparing for commercialization ahead of clearance, building our manufacturing capability, market access and commercial infrastructure in parallel with the regulatory process. That work continues as we prepare for launch. We expect to have enough capacity to support approximately 20,000 patients in the first year of launch. And we designed our manufacturing network to scale significantly as the launch expands. Fit is simply not another patch pump. It's the first of its kind, designed from the ground up with what patch consumers need.

    Patients have told us they want 3 things from a tubeless pump: longer wear, more insulin capacity and better automation. Fit is everything a tubeless system should be. Fit pairs up to 7 days of wear with a 300-unit insulin reservoir, so patients can change patches less often without giving up insulin capacity. It's app-controlled and designed to be waterproof. It keeps a persistent Bluetooth connection, so patients don't have to re-pair every new patch with their phone, and it can be worn in multiple places on the body. Fit also works with Simplera and Instinct and runs our SmartGuard algorithm. Until now, they've had to trade off one against another. With Fit, they don't.

    Industry observers note that that means fewer changes and less to think about with strong glucose control in a system that's easy to live with. We believe customers will feel the difference. And Fit is not the endpoint. It's designed to take wireless software updates, giving consumers a seamless path to Vivera, our fully closed-loop algorithm when it becomes available. As we discussed last quarter, Vivera is designed to eliminate carb counting or meal announcements while still delivering strong outcomes above the ADA guidelines of 70% time in range. We have fully enrolled our pivotal trial and are in the final stages of data collection.

    Industry observers note that based on our current timelines, we expect to submit Vivera to the FDA and report pivotal trial data in the first half of calendar year 2027, and we remain on track for a U.S. launch in the second half of calendar '27. Across the industry, most new competitor algorithms are built for one patient population and one style of use. That leaves patients and clinicians making trade-offs: simplicity or performance, hands-free or hands-on, type 1 or type 2, adult or pediatric, durable pump or patch pump. Our goal with Vivera was not to solve one of these trade-offs, it was to eliminate them. Diabetes is not one-size-fits-all. Needs differ between type 1 and type 2 and between adults and children.

    And even within these groups, they vary widely and change over time. Nowhere is this clearer than at mealtime. Carb counting is the last manual task in automated insulin delivery. And for 25 years, it has quietly decided who can use a pump. Other systems treat it as a switch, either you announce every meal or you give up control. Vivera treats it as a dial. Patients who want peak performance can choose to enter their meals. Patients who don't want to count carbs at all can skip it, and Vivera still delivers strong glucose control. Patients choose how to be involved at every meal, and that choice can change from one day to the next.

    Vivera is also designed for type 1 and type 2, children and adults at launch. We expect to offer it on Flex and Fit as a seamless over-the-air enhancement, so patients can choose a durable pump or patch pump without giving up algorithm performance. This flexibility in one algorithm took more than a decade of R&D, clinical research and simulation tools to build. The better the app automation, the broader the addressable population that will adopt AID therapy. Think of Vivera like a full self-driving car. The car drives, but you can take the wheel anytime you want, and that's exactly why people trust it enough to let it drive. Vivera works the same way.

    It handles insulin every 5 minutes, day and night. When you want even tighter control at a meal, you can enter carbs and take the wheel. When you don't, Vivera keeps driving. Other fully closed-loop systems work like a switch. Once it's on, you're a passenger. You only get what that algorithm can do on its own. And when something goes wrong, there's very little you can do about it. With Vivera, you never have to choose between letting go and getting the outcomes you deserve. Our sensor pipeline is moving too. Through our partnership with Abbott, we are integrating a dual glucose-ketone sensor into the MiniMed ecosystem.

    We expect to be the first to bring glucose and ketone monitoring together in one app with the sensor expected to launch with our new pumps next summer. Step back and the story isn't any single milestone. It's the momentum across the portfolio. A year ago, these programs were in development. Today, they are in pivotal trials, winning approvals and reaching patients. We're building the most complete platform for people who take insulin: Smart MDI, durable pump, patch pump and a choice of sensors, all connected by one algorithm and one digital ecosystem. And increasingly, we are no longer just building that platform. We are putting it in the hands of patients.

    It has been revealed that that innovation sits on a business that's getting stronger, demand is building, our underlying profitability is improving, and we just delivered our first quarter of positive free cash flow as an independent company. Flex, Fit, Go, Vivera and our sensor pipeline will expand the number of patients we serve from here. This is the strategy we laid out: deliver in our core business, expand the markets we serve, advance our pipeline and turn that growth into higher earnings and cash generation. Q2 was another meaningful step forward on every one of those priorities. With that, I'll turn it to Chad to walk through our Q2 financials and guidance.

    Sources indicate that chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Que. Q2 revenue was $822 million, up 9.4% on a reported basis and 9.7% organically, slightly ahead of organic growth expectations. As we said last quarter, we expected Q2 organic growth in both the U.S. and international to be similar to the underlying growth rates we delivered in Q1. That's what we delivered, with U.S. organic revenue growth of 8.3% and international organic revenue growth of 10.4%. Foreign currency lowered reported revenue by approximately $3 million in the quarter. Organic growth was strong across our portfolio, led by 15% growth in pumps and 10.8% growth in CGM. Pump growth was driven by our recent launches, including MiniMed Flex in the U.S.

    According to recent reports, globally, CGM growth was supported by greater sensor supply and continued adoption of Simplera and Instinct. Consumables grew 4.6% in the quarter and together with CGM, represent 81% of revenue, continue to provide a large and durable recurring revenue base. Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $140 million, up 19.7%, more than twice our reported revenue growth. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 17.0%, an increase of 150 basis points year-over-year. Walking through Q2 P&L, adjusted gross profit was $486 million, resulting in adjusted gross margin of 59.0%.

Despite that expected mix impact, gross margin continues to track meaningfully better than our assumptions, driven by continued improvement in Simplera yields. Adjusted SG&A was $285 million or 34.7% of revenue, growing 9.3% as we support our expanding commercial portfolio. We continue to invest behind our product launches while driving productivity across the organization. Adjusted R&D was $104 million, essentially flat year-over-year and represented 12.7% of revenue.

    R&D continued to provide operating leverage, reflecting productivity across regulatory, clinical, engineering and operations R&D and the progression of several major programs from development toward approval and commercialization. At the same time, we continue to invest in the next generation of MiniMed. Altogether, Q2 provides another clear proof point in the MiniMed business model. We can drive operating leverage and improve profitability while continuing to invest in the innovation and commercialization that supports our current and future growth. Turning to our key business metrics. Q2 new pumps sold or NPS, were 38,000, up 18% year-over-year and 11% from last quarter.

    Sources indicate that we ended Q2 with $256 million of cash, up $49 million from the prior quarter, no debt and a fully undrawn $500 million revolving credit facility. Our capital allocation priority remains investing in the business, and this liquidity gives us substantial flexibility to complete our separation, scale manufacturing capacity and fund our key growth opportunities. Q2 marked an important milestone in our cash generation. We generated $55 million of positive free cash flow, our first positive quarter as an independent company. This includes $31 million of separation and stand-up costs. Excluding those items, free cash flow was $86 million and operating cash flow was $146 million, demonstrating the underlying cash generation profile of the business today.

    As we have discussed, free cash flow may vary from quarter to quarter over the next year and may not be positive every quarter while we continue to incur these one-time separation-related costs. Importantly, excluding these temporary separation-related items, we expect the underlying business to remain free cash flow positive. We expect separation and stand-up costs to largely end by the close of calendar 2027. As these costs roll off and revenue and profitability grow, we expect the business to generate significant positive free cash flow. Next, let's cover our outlook for the remainder of fiscal 2027. We are maintaining our fiscal 2027 organic revenue growth outlook of approximately 10.5%.

    According to recent reports, this outlook continues to include the 1 to 1.5 percentage points benefit from the extra week in Q1. Over the rest of the year, we continue to expect our recent product launches to add more to revenue and revenue growth. For the second half of fiscal 2027, we expect U.S. and international organic growth to remain broadly consistent with Q2 levels. Strong demand, faster growth in new pumps sold and continued product launch momentum and strength across our markets give us confidence in our full year outlook. Turning to Fit. We're very encouraged by FDA clearance and our accelerated launch timeline. As we've discussed before, pharmacy access and formulary coverage take time to build.

    It has been revealed that starting next spring, we expect Fit to be an notable driver of upcoming pumps sold and installed base growth. Its contribution to revenue and profit will be smaller initially and build over the first 18 to 24 months as we gain formulary access and scale manufacturing capacity. Over time, a growing base of Fit customers creates long-term recurring revenue from ongoing patch pump and CGM use, which we expect to drive meaningful profit growth and our outlook continues to reflect this ramp. Turning to profitability. Our strong Q2 performance reinforces our confidence in the underlying earnings outlook for the business.

    And now with the earlier-than-expected FDA clearance of Fit, we expect to pull forward manufacturing, sales and marketing investments that were previously planned for future periods to accelerate the launch in the spring. Our Q2 outperformance gives us the capacity to fund these incremental fiscal 2027 investments while reaffirming our adjusted EBITDA margin guidance. Absent the accelerated Fit investments, the underlying strength of the business would have supported increasing our operating outlook. As we indicated last quarter, excluding the Blackstone Fit charge, we expect a larger portion of the full year EBITDA improvement to occur in the second half. Before I turn it back to Que, let me provide a brief update on our separation progress. To accelerate adoption, these technologies need to be simpler and less burdensome for people living with diabetes and the healthcare professionals who support them.

    Sources indicate that that is why we believe the future of our industry will be defined not by who serves today's pump users, but by who can bring advanced therapy to the millions of people who are not benefiting from it today. And I think -- in general, I think you agree that competitive bidding is not a good thing for the industry as a whole. It's -- the Medicare business for us is single-digit number of our overall business. So this is something that we expect to withstand. And so when we look at our overall portfolio, we've got MiniMed Fit going through pharmacy, our CGMs available through pharmacy. And as the pumps -- that mix goes -- increases through pharmacy, we expect that there will be price opportunities with that channel in the U.S.

    We continue to advocate for choice and access with the administration with CMS as they go through the details in rolling this out. I think the rental model is still -- there are details to be figured out. Given that the devices in this space are single-use devices, renting them out is -- there are certain barriers that we have to overcome. So I think there's still details to be figured out. So we're managing this. And the fact that we have the strength of this portfolio with all these upcoming products opening up the pharmacy channel, I think that helps us -- it provides a number of levers to offset challenges that competitive bidding may provide.

    Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Pasquale with Barclays.

    Recent findings suggest that christopher (Chris) Pasquale: I wanted to ask about Vivera. You talked a lot about choice as a key design consideration. Owners can pick and choose how they interact with the algorithm, which certainly adds a lot of flexibility. But does that mean that the training required to get new users comfortable with the system will be more involved than it will be for algorithms that just don't give them as many options since they've got to be comfortable with all the different ways they can use it? And how do you think about what that means for the ability of non-endocrinologists to prescribe it?

    Sources indicate that que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Chris. We actually designed it to be very easy to onboard onto therapy. All you need is your total daily dose. So if you're on an MDI, you know what your total daily dose is, that's all you need to enter therapy. There are no settings to be done by the physician. You don't need to do any programming. It's as close to self-start as you can get. So the training is extremely simple. So that's Vivera, and it's designed to really eliminate carb counting, but not sacrifice outcomes. So we want people to be above 70% time in range without needing to carb count whatsoever.

    Now a lot of the feedback we hear from patients though is when you have something like a forced full closed loop that we hear from some of our competitors, people are nervous about that because they don't know how it's going to perform. It may not get you to 70% time in range. And if you get into a sticky situation, there's not much you can do because there's no -- there aren't any levers to pull. You're in a forced full closed system. In our system, if you want tighter control, you can input and say something like, "I'm eating," or you can put in a carb count.

    In a recent development, and the system will also take that input and give you better control. And so we've really designed it to accommodate the full spectrum: people who don't want to do anything and people who do. And one algorithm can handle all of that. And I think that actually builds trust because just like in our commentary, the car analogy, a lot of people are nervous about going to a self-driving car because it's quite a foreign concept.

    But once you're in one and you see how it works and if you can take control at any time, you're more likely to trust that system than trust your health to a forced algorithm that can only get to a certain maximum, doesn't get you out of trouble should you get into those sort of tricky corners.

    Christopher (Chris) Pasquale: That's helpful. And then the announcement on the dual glucose-ketone sensor was an interesting update. Curious how you think about who across your user base that is going to appeal to.

    Que Thanh Dallara: Look, I think it's still early days with how to use the ketone information. I think we're very excited to be the first. We believe the first app that's going to incorporate ketone and glucose on the same screen. I think the other implementation you're going to see in the market will have 2 apps. You've got your CGM app that may have -- that will have the ketone on it and then you've got the pump app, and we're going to integrate that all into one. So I think it still is something that needs to be studied.

    But I think for people who want the bells and whistles and additional information, they would be attracted to the ketone sensor. We hear a lot of interest from pediatric accounts that it's sort of belts and suspenders for parents. And so, but it's still early days in terms of that user experience. There's more to be studied. But by having all that information onto the one app, I think we're simplifying the experience for providers and for patients. And I think that facilitates what else can you do with ketones and where can that be helpful into the future. But certainly, on peds accounts, for example, I think it will be a very strong value proposition with our system.

    Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Joanne Wuensch with Citi.

    In a recent development, joanne Wuensch: It seems like the Vivera algorithm will be available after the launch of Fit. Can you sort of walk through how you think about sort of post hoc adding that into the systems? And then my second question is, is there a way to measure the percentage of revenue that's going through the pharmacy today? And is there a goal for what that might look like in the future?

    Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Joanne. On Vivera, it will be a simple over-the-air upgrade. As you know, when you get a Flex pump, it's really less than 10 minutes to upgrade the firmware and get the latest software update, and it will be the same with MiniMed Fit as well as MiniMed Flex. So very simple over-the-air update. So as soon as Vivera is cleared, and we're preparing for launch, we can push that to all our customers and all the devices. So it's pretty seamless. In terms of the pharmacy channel, today, our pharmacy mix is relatively low in the single-digit category. We haven't given you a number. I think, obviously, we've got massive ambitions to increase that.

    In a recent development, we're pretty excited with Fit exclusively going through pharmacy in the U.S. And so I think as that ramps, we'll be able to share more in the future.

    Industry observers note that chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Daniel. Yes, gross margin execution, it's really around -- the main factor is Simplera, right? So that's a huge driver. We're seeing benefits in our warranty. So as our products get more and more reliable, our warranty costs are getting even better than we anticipated. We're seeing manufacturing variance favorability across the board and even favorable PPV. So really, it's really strong execution across everything manufacturing from a gross margin standpoint.

    Industry observers note that so that's great news, right, from where we anticipated being. And then as we think of the evolution, we talk about all the fresh product rolls out. So Simplera is an example of something that you need to build significant scale to get to profitability, we're getting better.     Industry observers note that as we think of the patch pump, it's going to obviously have a lower gross margin as we spoke about earlier, given the things that we're doing to get on formulary and as the scale needs to build up.     Latest Update: Netflix Stock Is Down 37% in 2026, But the Business Is Still Growing. Here's Why I'd Buy It Before the End of November.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that media-streaming veteran Netflix (NFLX +1.32%) is on the outs with Wall Street again.
    • And the more I look at the drooping stock chart, the more I scratch my head in confusion.
    • Third-quarter results did not look like those of a firm in trouble.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Anders Bylund – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:07PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Netflix ›.

    Sources indicate that media-streaming veteran Netflix (NFLX +1.32%) is on the outs with Wall Street again. The stock reached all-time highs in the summer of 2025, as investors forgave the company for the canceled, expensive Warner Bros. buyout idea. As of Nov. 24, Netflix stock is down 56% from that peak, including a 37% year-to-date drop.

    And the more I look at the drooping stock chart, the more I scratch my head in confusion. The business keeps growing, video streaming remains a healthy global market, and Netflix's stock isn't even expensive.

    Third-quarter results did not look like those of a firm in trouble. Revenue rose 11.8% to $12.9 billion. Operating income jumped 37.3% to $4.5 billion, and operating margin widened to 34.6% from 28.2% in the year-ago period. Management guided for 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion, up 13%, and an operating margin of 31.5%, versus 29.5% in 2025. That's a combo of double-digit revenue growth and widening margins.

    Investors sold anyway. The stock fell as much as 6.7% the next morning, and several analysts trimmed their price targets. At first glance, the reasons look fair. Netflix cut its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from roughly $3 billion to about $2.7 billion, citing slower rollout of some upcoming ad products. Ad revenue is still on pace to grow more than 80% this year, per co-CEO Greg Peters. Management conceded, though, that view-hour growth needs to improve and that the U.S. content group can do better.

    Recent findings suggest that "Our [U.S.] engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years, but we know that we can do better. And that better is our upside," Peters remarked on the earnings call. "It's our goal to go from very good to great on the performance of that slate.".

    Industry observers note that now check the stock's price tag. Netflix's market cap is about $238.6 billion. Tack on $7.1 billion of net debt, and the whole enterprise costs about 15.8 times the operating income it generated over the past four quarters. That's a low multiple for a organization that turned 31.3% of its revenue into operating income over the past year. Take a quick look at the price chart and you'd assume the business was shrinking. Well, it's not.

    Management has been voting with the checkbook, so to speak. Netflix bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion last quarter (a company record, narrowly edging the Q2 buyback budget) at an average of about $75 per stub. The stock now sits around $59, so the timing could have been better. Still, $22.3 billion of buyback authorization remains, against $8.2 billion of cash and about $12.0 billion of expected 2026 free cash flow. Netflix has leaned harder into buybacks as the stock has slid this year, and the remaining authorization leaves room for more:.

    NFLX data by YCharts. The chart indicates quarterly buybacks; Netflix reported $4.8 billion for Q3 2026.

    In a recent development, wall Street has not given up on the story. The analyst consensus rating is Buy, and short-sellers hold roughly 2% of Netflix's shares, a thin bearish bet against the stock.

    Recent findings suggest that the fourth quarter should keep the content engine busy. Netflix calls it the biggest quarterly live slate it has ever scheduled, including its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game on Nov. 25. That game kicks off a stretch of live events that could shift sentiment fast: a Christmas Day football doubleheader and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua heavyweight boxing event. Self-produced entertainment releases include "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a fresh season of "The Diplomat," and the sixth and final run of "Emily in Paris.".

    It has been revealed that netflix also looks to launch its advertising tier in 15 more countries next year, starting in March. It recently named former Disney (DIS +1.86%) executive Peter Rice as chief content officer. Regional hits matter, too; Netflix has a deep bench of local producers, and their shows are moving the needle. For instance, India view hours grew 24% in the third quarter while revenue there rose about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    I can't pretend that Netflix is a risk-free investment. Some new ad products are behind schedule. Fourth-quarter margin guidance of 26% absorbs about 120 basis points of cost from headcount cuts. Operating income is guided to about $3.5 billion, up 18.4% from a year ago, and that's a sharp slowdown from the third quarter's 37.3% jump. The U.S. slate needs to start landing home runs instead of base hits, which is exactly the job Peter Rice just inherited. So no, you shouldn't bet the farm, the cat, and the horse it rode in on. A normal slice of a diversified portfolio is plenty.

    But a growing, cash-generating business at about 16 times operating income, with a Buy consensus and almost nobody shorting it? That's why I'd buy Netflix now, rather than wait for the holiday slate to change the market mood. The stock may keep sliding in the short term; the business, so far, is not.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Joe Tenebruso – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:21PM EST.

    Many of your stocks are likely to disappoint you.

    It's a sobering statement, but one that's borne out by decades of stock market returns.

    In a recent development, research from J.P. Morgan going back to 1980 indicates that two-thirds of the stocks in the Russell 3000, which is designed to track the performance of the largest 3,000 publicly traded U.S. companies, tend to underperform the index.

    Worse still, roughly 40% of stocks had negative absolute returns.

    Moreover, a report from Trivariate Research suggests that an even larger percentage of companies underperformed in recent years, with just 23% of stocks beating the S&P 500 over the past decade.

    In a recent development, at first glance, this data is pretty disheartening. Investing may not be easy, but this research makes it seem nearly impossible to be successful.

    The truth, fortunately, is that it's not.

    There's a beautiful asymmetry to investing.

    It's true that a stock could lose 100% of its value. Enduring such a loss is not pleasant. But a well-chosen stock can gain 200%, 500%, or even 1,000% or more.

    This capped downside and uncapped upside is part of the magic of investing. As long as you don't use leverage (such as buying stocks on margin), a few big winners can more than make up for a host of losers.

    While the odds may be against you, it's still possible to find stocks that go on to outperform the market averages.

    The most valuable suggestion I can give you is to buy shares in the best businesses you can find.

    In a recent development, search for companies with the strongest competitive advantages and largest growth opportunities. This includes those with proven business models, beloved brands, superior products and services, and excellent management. Even better if they also possess powerful network effects, high barriers to entry, and sizable switching costs.

    Look for the innovators, disruptors, and best of breed. I call these businesses Tier 1 enterprises, and finding just a handful of them can set you up for a lifetime of investment success.

    It has been revealed that to achieve those life-changing returns, you'll need to keep them long enough to maximize their impact on your wealth. This is one reason why Warren Buffett claims his "favorite holding period is forever.".

    Strive to purchase only shares of businesses you strategy to hold for many years. This will lead you to focus on companies with the strongest competitive positions and widest economic moats, or those you believe will eventually build them.

    Sources indicate that still, despite your best efforts, you will make mistakes. Don't let them derail you.

    A stock you thought was a sure winner will fail. Recessions will slow the greatest of growth stories. Bear markets will bring fear, uncertainty, and doubt. Even your own emotions may betray you.

    Sources indicate that come what may, don't quit. Steel yourself with the knowledge that the hard times will pass and you will get through them.

    Recent findings suggest that learn from your mistakes. Apply the lessons to your future stock selections.

    Continuously refine your investing process until you obtain the results you need to provide for yourself and your family and achieve your financial freedom.

    Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

    📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.
    • Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.
    • The visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

    Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

    The visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

    LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU.

    Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

    Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

    Recent findings suggest that “We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

    “We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”.

    When Wolverhampton Wanderers last attacked the Championship under a Portuguese manager new to English football, it proved a vintage season.

    Molineux was under the spell of Nuno Espírito Santo in that 2017-18 campaign, and the big question is whether César Peixoto can lead a repeat nearly a decade later.

    Peixoto was a surprise appointment in June, replacing Rob Edwards, and he has been entrusted with the mission of returning Wolves to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

    It has been revealed that “I have changed some things with set-pieces and some things in other moments of the game because I want the team to be organised and understand all the different moments within a match. During pre-season we have scored some goals from high pressing, but we will not be able to press high in every moment of every game. The players have to understand the game and recognise what each moment requires. It is notable that we work as a team. When we can press high, we’ll press high. When we need to defend in a mid-block, we will stay organised. When the opposition pushes us deeper, which will sometimes happen, we have to be organised there as well.

    According to recent reports, “There are a lot of crosses in the Championship, for example, so the team needs to understand what to do in those situations. We want to play our football, be offensive and react strongly when we lose the ball, but we also need to understand the different moments of the game. I think we are at a good level to attack the Championship.”.

    Sources indicate that the 2026/27 Championship season kicks off at Molineux as Wolves host Blackburn, with the home side hoping to put the bad memories of last season firmly behind them. There are newly introduced playoff rules in place for this season, with six places now up for grabs in the play-offs.

    Industry observers note that wolves are aiming to return to the Premier League at the first attempt, having endured a miserable season in the top flight last year as they finished bottom with just three wins to their name. It has been a summer of change at the club as they chose to change managers. Rob Edwards lost his job in what was a shock move and was replaced by 46-year-old Cesar Peixoto, with this being his first head coaching position outside of his home country Portugal. Back in 2017/18, Wolves won the Championship title led by Peixoto’s compatriot Nuno Espirito Santo.

    In a recent development, “I am ready,” Peixoto told Wolves’ club website. “We have worked very hard during pre-season, and I think we have had a great pre-season. All the players have worked very, very hard and they understand what I want from them. I am ready and confident going into the first game. Football is football, whether it is in Portugal or England, but there are different characteristics to the game here. We have watched, observed and analysed the Championship. We did that work before I came to the club, so we know what to expect.

    “It is going to be a tough season with good teams, but we are prepared to fight for the three points game after game and week after week. We know what we want from the team and we know what our major goal is. We’re going to work very hard and fight to achieve that goal.”.

    It has been revealed that they have brought in vast experience on the player side in the shape of Kieran Trippier and Raul Jimenez, who is back at Molineux three years after leaving for Fulham. Although they have lost Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes to Aston Villa, most of their squad has stayed intact as they pursue promotion back to the top flight. It is a special year for the club as they celebrate their 150th anniversary.

    Blackburn, led by experienced manager Tony Mowbray, did not enjoy a great season in the Championship last year, finishing down in 20th place and just five points above the relegation zone. 14 years have now passed since Blackburn last played in the top flight.

    “I think it is a tough start,” Mowbray said. “On paper, I would suggest the first couple of games, particularly, jumped out as a tough start. One of the Premier League sides from last season, away from home. They have got a very talented squad, a pretty expensive squad. They have got some very good individual talent. Yet, there is an argument to say they have not won many football matches in the last calendar year. So, what we get, we will have to wait and see.”.

    Recent findings suggest that these sides last met in the FA Cup during the 2024/25 season, with Wolves winning that fourth-round tie 2-0 thanks to goals from Matheus Cunha and Gomes, both of whom are now plying their trade elsewhere. The omens would appear to be on Wolves’ side as they are unbeaten in their last eight league meetings with Blackburn. Both sides progressed to the second round of the League Cup last weekend, with Wolves beating Port Vale 3-0 and Blackburn overcoming Burton Albion 2-1.

    What is the legal betting age in the US?

    The minimum age depends on the jurisdiction and product. Many sportsbooks require customers to be 21 or older. Some markets allow sports betting at 18. Check both the sportsbook's age requirement and the terms of the promotion you plan to claim.

    Do I have to pay taxes on sports betting winnings?

    Sources indicate that yes. The IRS requires you to report gambling winnings even if you receive no Form W-2G. Keep records of your wagers and payouts for tax reporting.

    What happens to my NFL player prop if a player gets injured?

    Check the market's participation and injury rules. At DraftKings, Early Exit Protected can void eligible full-game props when a player leaves injured in the first half and never returns. In an eligible parlay, DraftKings removes the voided leg and recalculates the odds on the remaining selections.

    Are sports betting apps safe to use?

    Verify the operator on your state regulator's licensed sportsbook list and download the official app. Check how to set deposit limits, take a break or self-exclude before funding an account. Wagers can lose even when the operator is licensed.

    Decide how much you can afford to spend before opening the bet slip. Treat that amount as a limit and avoid increasing it to qualify for a promotion. If gambling is causing problems, support is available through the National Council on Problem Gambling.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:26PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    Industry observers note that shares of Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) reached a 52-week high on Oct. 6, but they have dropped by a remarkable 31% since then, as investors pressed the panic button for multiple reasons.

    Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation (before he was reinstated on Nov. 23), an investigation into Nvidia's dealings in China, and a reported probe by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) into the firm's accounting practices have sent the stock packing over the past month and a half. The negativity surrounding Nvidia stock was so severe that even its quarterly results and better-than-expected guidance didn't arrest its slide.

    Sources indicate that however, Nvidia rallied over 31% following Huang’s reappointment, suggesting that investor confidence in the stock could improve. What’s more, the last time Nvidia witnessed such a sharp pullback in a short period, it went on a multi-year rally. Let's take a look at what happened in 2018.

    Nvidia stock fell 54% between October and December 2018. This massive slide was triggered by an oversupply in the graphics processing unit (GPU) market, driven by a drop in cryptocurrency-related sales. Additionally, the manufacturer was caught up in a broader sell-off of tech stocks at the time.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Sources indicate that nvidia's growth slowed as crypto-driven GPU demand faded, leaving the tech giant with excess inventory. In fact, Nvidia's revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2019 (which ended in January 2019) fell 24% year over year to $2.2 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings dropped by 53% from the year-ago period during the quarter.

    It has been revealed that investors decided to book profits in Nvidia stock following stellar returns in 2016 and 2017. Nvidia lost 31% of its value in 2018. For comparison, it jumped by 227% in 2016 and 82% in 2017. So, this isn't the first time that Nvidia stock has lost its wheels and undergone a significant correction in a short time.

    According to recent reports, however, what's worth noting is that Nvidia went on a stunning bull run starting in 2019, driven by multiple catalysts, including strong GPU sales during the novel coronavirus pandemic and the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in late 2022. Nvidia stock has jumped by a whopping 4,740% since the beginning of 2019.

    Industry observers note that so, savvy investors who saw the long-term opportunity in Nvidia's shares at that time are sitting on massive gains right now, even after the stock's recent sell-off. What's more, a closer look at Nvidia's valuation suggests that it is way more attractive right now than it was in 2018.

    What a $5,000 Investment in Shopify Stock Today Could Grow Into by 2030

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Shopify (SHOP -1.48%) stock climbed around 9% on Monday, Nov.
    • The holiday shopping season, normally the e-commerce company's biggest stretch of the year, kicks off with Black Friday on Nov.
    • In a recent development, at roughly $134 per share as I write, $5,000 buys about 37 shares.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:43PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Shopify ›.

    Shopify (SHOP -1.48%) stock climbed around 9% on Monday, Nov. 23, closing at $134.30. Still, shares are down about 17% in 2026, and they'd have to rise about 33% to get back to the $179.22 record hit on Oct. 12.

    The holiday shopping season, normally the e-commerce company's biggest stretch of the year, kicks off with Black Friday on Nov. 27.

    In a recent development, at roughly $134 per share as I write, $5,000 buys about 37 shares. By my math, those shares might be worth about $6,800 at the end of 2030. That'd be a gain of about $1,800, or roughly 8% a year.

    In a recent development, the estimate has Shopify's free cash flow per share more than doubling by 2030, even as growth cools. It also assumes investors will pay far less for every dollar of that cash flow than they do today, at about 65 times free cash flow.

    Sources indicate that after two straight quarters of 34% growth earlier in 2026, Shopify's revenue climbed 32% year over year in the third quarter, to around $3.7 billion. Management sees growth at a low-thirties percentage rate again in the fourth quarter, with gross profit growing at a high-twenties rate.

    Free cash flow (the cash left after capital spending) has mostly kept pace with revenue, because Shopify's free cash flow margin hasn't changed much. Shopify kept 18% of its revenue as free cash flow in 2024 and 17% in 2025. Over the last four quarters, the number was around 19%, helped by a 22% third quarter. Management expects the fourth-quarter margin to match the 19% it reported a year before.

    If fourth-quarter revenue rises around 31% at that margin, Shopify would finish 2026 with about $15.3 billion in revenue, up 32% from 2025, and about $2.9 billion in free cash flow, up around 40%. Spread over the third quarter's 1.29 billion diluted shares, that's around $2.20 of free cash flow per share.

    The share count has been dropping, too. Shopify bought back around $2.5 billion of its stock in the first nine months of 2026, and its third-quarter diluted share count was down about 2% from a year earlier.

    I've assumed revenue growth keeps slowing, from the low 30s now to the mid-teens by 2030, averaging about 20% a year from 2027 through 2030. That would put 2030 revenue around $32 billion, about twice this year's likely total.

    It has been revealed that if free cash flow holds just below 19% of revenue, where it should land in 2026, Shopify would produce almost $6 billion of it in 2030. And I've kept the share count near 1.29 billion, though buybacks have been lowering it. That puts 2030 free cash flow at around $4.60 per share, a little over twice this year's $2.20.

    Shopify's market cap is about $173 billion at $134.30, putting the shares at about 65 times free cash flow. At its October record, Shopify fetched about 98 times free cash flow. And even at its lowest close in 2026, about $95 on May 13, it went for roughly 59 times free cash flow.

    I've assumed 40 times free cash flow at the end of 2030. That's still a premium price, and it looks fair for a business that could be growing in the mid-teens by then. But it's far below anything investors have paid for Shopify this year.

    At 40 times free cash flow, $4.60 per share gives a stock price around $184. Thirty-seven shares at that price are worth about $6,800.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Of course, another free cash flow multiple would change the result a lot. If investors still paid 65 times free cash flow in 2030, the $5,000 would grow to about $11,100. At 30 times free cash flow, it would be worth about $5,100, barely more than what went in.

    According to recent reports, shopify's business looks healthy enough to keep growing its cash flow at an impressive rate. But my base case comes out to roughly 8% a year, and a less generous valuation in 2030 might erase most of that gain. This year alone, shares have closed as low as about $95 and as high as about $179.

    With swings like that, I'd want a lower starting price before putting $5,000 into Shopify stock.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, tech stocks slid again on Tuesday, and some of the market's most famous investors have been positioning for that kind of drop.
    • The bets use put options, which give the holder the right to sell at a set price and generally rise in value when the underlying investment falls.
    • Paul Singer's Elliott Investment Management held puts on 5.46 million shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -1.99%), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, according to its latest 13F.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:48PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›.

    In a recent development, tech stocks slid again on Tuesday, and some of the market's most famous investors have been positioning for that kind of drop. Quarterly filings show that two billionaire-run firms added big bets against the Nasdaq-100 during the third quarter.

    The bets use put options, which give the holder the right to sell at a set price and generally rise in value when the underlying investment falls. The filings, called 13Fs, were made with the SEC on Nov. 16 and show holdings as of Sept. 30.

    Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

    Paul Singer's Elliott Investment Management held puts on 5.46 million shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -1.99%), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, according to its latest 13F. The filing values them at $4.04 billion, with only its Phillips 66 and Triple Flag Precious Metals stakes representing a bigger value.

    Recent findings suggest that importantly, that figure is the value of the shares the puts cover, rather than what Elliott paid for them or what it could make. The filing doesn't show the strike prices or expiration dates, so the size of the actual bet is unknown.

    Industry observers note that three months earlier, Elliott held puts on 3.48 million QQQ shares, valued at $2.56 billion, according to its prior filing. It also raised its puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -7.26%) to 800,000 shares from 250,000, covering $487 million of shares.

    Sources indicate that but Elliott isn't only betting against tech. It also reported puts covering $1.27 billion of an industrials fund, $903 million of a consumer staples fund, and $865 million of a gold miners fund. It cut its puts on a technology-software fund nearly in half, to $873 million. As a whole, the spread looks more like protection across the whole market than a single bet against tech.

    According to recent reports, paul Tudor Jones' Tudor Investment held QQQ puts covering 8.55 million shares valued at $6.32 billion, according to its 13F. That's up from 4.74 million shares, or $3.49 billion, in its prior filing.

    However, Tudor also raised its QQQ calls, which gain when the fund rises, to 7.75 million shares, or $5.74 billion. So its puts outweigh its calls, but not by much. Its biggest bearish line wasn't tech at all: puts on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks smaller companies, covering $8.75 billion of shares.

    Industry observers note that separately, Stanley Druckenmiller isn't betting against tech, but he isn't betting on it either. He told the TomorrowX conference in Austin this month that he's "taking a break" from stocks and is close to neutral on equities while he waits for a clearer outlook.

    Not much. These filings have real limits. Besides omitting strike prices and costs, a 13F doesn't show short sales or positions in securities outside U.S.-listed securities. A put can be an outright bet on a decline, or it can be insurance for a firm that owns a lot of stocks. Both Elliott and Tudor hold billions in other positions that those puts may be protecting.

    The data is also somewhat stale. The filings show positions as of Sept. 30, and these firms trade often. Any of them could have changed by now.

    What the filings do show is that experienced investors are paying for protection, especially against tech stocks and the broader Nasdaq. For long-term investors, the takeaway isn't to sell. Instead, check how much of the portfolio rides on a handful of names (particularly AI names), and make sure it's an amount they can live with if selling continues.

    According to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the average price of a can of soda in the U.S. is around $0.60 when bought as part of a 12-pack -- up 80% from its price in 2019. While this is an extreme example, it highlights the devastating impact inflation can have on your purchasing power and the real value of your stock market returns.

    Unfortunately for investors, inflation remains a problem. And a devastating warning from President Donald Trump suggests it could get worse before it gets better. Let's dig deeper into the market's challenges and discuss strategies investors can use to stay ahead of the curve.

    For many investors, the Trump era has been a bit of a headscratcher. The administration has deliberately pursued disruptive policies, such as massive tariffs that can make it harder for many U.S. companies to do business. But instead of crashing, stocks have gone gangbusters, with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.50%) jumping 25% since his election victory in November.

    To be fair, some of this is luck. Trump has been in the right place at the right time to oversee the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), which has single-handedly added trillions to the value of America's tech industry. That mentioned, White House policies have also played a role.

    Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act helped lock in corporate tax cuts while also slashing regulations in the energy industry and introducing goodies such as allowing companies to write off certain categories of research and development expenses for tax purposes. Big tech is also happy with the administration's generally pro-AI stance, which is crucial at a time when public pushback against data center construction is growing.

    That remarked, while Trump has managed to keep Wall Street happy so far, the administration has struggled to rein in other macroeconomic challenges that could undermine investor returns over the long haul. The biggest challenge is inflation. Tariffs and the Iran war have helped push the U.S. inflation rate to around 4% as of October, which is well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.

    Higher inflation hurts investors' real returns and encourages the central bank to continue raising interest rates. This generally hurts stock valuations by making it harder for businesses to access the capital they need to invest in future growth.

    Image source: Official White House Photo.

    Industry observers note that when asked about the situation earlier last month, Trump's response was alarming. In an interview with Time magazine, he suggested "certain levels of inflation" could help pay down the national debt "very rapidly." The logic may be that by lowering the value of the dollar, inflation will also devalue America's $40 trillion in borrowings, making it easier to manage. These remarks suggest the White House is willing to tolerate high inflation for much longer than investors will be comfortable with.

    Sources indicate that trump's warning suggests that the U.S. government doesn't have a strong strategy to bring down inflation or manage the national debt. In fact, both of these problems could get worse over the coming months as the war in Iran (along with the war in Ukraine) continues to drive up military spending and create lasting bottlenecks in the global economy.

    In a recent development, that mentioned, this isn't the time to panic. And it can pay to look toward the wisdom of investing legend Warren Buffett, who advised investors to never bet against America in his annual shareholder letter during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. Over the long haul, the country has consistently bounced back from crises only to emerge stronger than ever. And there is no reason to assume this time will be the exception.

    The recent midterm results have also already eased fears in the oil markets, as many traders expect the latest Democrat-controlled Congress to impose more checks and balances on Trump's foreign policy.

    According to recent reports, the economic situation remains uncertain, but the long-term outlook is bright. And investors can stay ahead by increasing portfolio diversification to avoid being overly exposed to underperformance in any specific asset class.

    Breaking: Anthropic Has Plunged 30% From Its Peak. Here’s the Price at Which I’d Buy.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, following months of anticipation, artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public market debut on Nov.
    • Indeed, Anthropic's revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate.
    • Let's explore what's driving the sell-off in Anthropic stock and assess the valuation at which the company could become a compelling investment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adam Spatacco – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    In a recent development, following months of anticipation, artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public market debut on Nov. 19. While the maker of Claude initially received an enthusiastic reception, the excitement has been short-lived. Less than a week after going public, Anthropic stock has already started selling off.

    Indeed, Anthropic's revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate. But smart investors are not overlooking the capital-intensive nature underpinning the firm's expansion. Furthermore, competition across the large language model (LLM) landscape raises important questions about Anthropic's path to profitability.

    Let's explore what's driving the sell-off in Anthropic stock and assess the valuation at which the company could become a compelling investment.

    In a recent development, anthropic completed the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, surpassing the $75 billion raised by Space Exploration Technologies back in June. Including the full exercise of the underwriters' option to purchase additional shares, Anthropic's IPO generated $93.5 billion in gross proceeds.

    Industry observers note that the company also completed a concurrent $26 billion private placement involving Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Micron Technology. Combined gross proceeds from the two transactions reached $119.5 billion.

    When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq, shares opened at $111.50, or about 34% above the offering price of $83. Shares subsequently climbed to an intraday high of $115.10 before reversing course and closing their first day of trading at $97.17. As of this writing (Nov. 24), Anthropic stock is hovering around $80, representing a decline of 30% from its high.

    Some of the selling pressure likely reflects momentum traders locking in profits, but attributing the entire decline to short-term trading overlooks several important fundamental concerns.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic's growth is difficult to dispute. According to its S-1 filing, the manufacturer generated approximately $17 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing 1,127% growth year over year. Furthermore, Anthropic ended October with an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion.

    Revenue growth is only one part of Anthropic's financial profile. The company has $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments, including $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before Dec. 31, 2030.

    While these obligations shouldn't be confused with conventional debt, they illustrate the capital requirements required to develop and operate frontier AI models. Anthropic's ability to generate sustainable profits depends heavily on whether customer demand and premium pricing can justify these investments.

    Anthropic competes against OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's Gemini, Meta's Muse, and an expanding ecosystem of open-weight models. As generative models become more sophisticated and less expensive to operate, Anthropic may face pressure to lower its prices while continuing to invest aggressively in computing capacity.

    Unlike Alphabet or Meta Platforms, Anthropic doesn't have a mature, highly profitable advertising or cloud computing business that generates cash to help subsidize its AI infrastructure investments. As a result, investors are being asked to place enormous amounts of faith in Anthropic's ability to translate its revenue growth into durable earnings and free cash flow at some point in the future.

    Given Anthropic's lack of profitability, a traditional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio isn't particularly useful in this analysis. Instead, I'd value the organization relative to its annualized revenue run rate. At $80 per share, Anthropic's market capitalization is roughly $1.1 trillion. This equates to 13.5 times its annualized revenue run rate from October.

    I am more interested in Anthropic stock at $50 per share. At that price, the manufacturer would boast an implied market cap of about $690 billion, equivalent to 8.5 times its annualized revenue run rate. Anthropic's growth could allow the company to grow into this valuation relatively swiftly. For example, if its annualized revenue run rate doubles to roughly $160 billion, a $690 billion valuation would represent just 4.3 times that figure.

    According to recent reports, with that mentioned, investors shouldn't assume Anthropic's current growth trajectory will last indefinitely. Moreover, the company will need to demonstrate that its revenue can fuel sustainable free cash flow despite its infrastructure commitments.

    Sources indicate that although Anthropic is one of the most premier businesses leading the AI revolution, an exciting company doesn't always make an attractive stock at every price. At $50 per share, I'd be more comfortable initiating a modest position and gradually building exposure as Anthropic makes progress toward profitability. Until then, I think patience is warranted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A pair of quarterbacks from the fabled 2004 draft class, Pittsburgh Steelers legend Ben Roethlisberger and Latest York Giants icon Eli Manning, plus embattled wide receiver Antonio Brown, are among the 52 players the Pro Football Hall of Fame revealed are advancing in the voting process for the 2027 class.

    • The list the Hall declared on Tuesday will next be cut down to 25 players.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A pair of quarterbacks from the fabled 2004 draft class, Pittsburgh Steelers legend Ben Roethlisberger and Latest York Giants icon Eli Manning, plus embattled wide receiver Antonio Brown, are among the 52 players the Pro Football Hall of Fame revealed are advancing in the voting process for the 2027 class.

    Per current Hall of Fame bylaws, at this stage of that process, selectors cast ballots for 50 players they believe should move forward in their candidacy, but those tied for the 50th position also remain eligible for induction.

    The list the Hall declared on Tuesday will next be cut down to 25 players. That more exclusive group will be unveiled in about two weeks.

    For now, here's a position-by-position breakdown of the players being considered for enshrinement:.

    Ben Roethlisberger, Eli Manning, Ken Anderson.

    Shaun Alexander, Frank Gore, Marshawn Lynch, LeSean McCoy, Adrian Peterson, Fred Taylor, Ricky Watters.

    Anquan Boldin, Antonio Brown, Rob Gronkowski, Torry Holt, Billy "White Shoes" Johnson, Steve Smith Sr., Otis Taylor, Hines Ward, Reggie Wayne, Jason Witten.

    Rodney Harrison, Lester Hayes, Albert Lewis, Eddie Meador, Richard Sherman, Earl Thomas III, Everson Walls, Darren Woodson.

    John Abraham, Geno Atkins, L.C. Greenwood, Jim Marshall, Robert Mathis, Haloti Ngata, Vince Wilfork, Kevin Williams.

    Maxie Baughan, London Fletcher, James Harrison, Karl Mecklenburg, Tommy Nobis, Terrell Suggs.

    Roethlisberger and Manning draw the eye, considering they each quarterbacked historic franchises to a pair of Super Bowl victories; however, this cohort is understandably littered with household names.

    Recent findings suggest that running back Adrian Peterson is forever part of Minnesota Vikings lore. He's one of the nine NFL players to ever rush for 2,000 yards in a season. In fact, Peterson's 2,097 yards on the ground in 2012 were the second most in a single-season in league history, behind only the 2,105 rushing yards Eric Dickerson logged while starring for the Los Angeles Rams in 1984. Peterson earned NFL MVP honors that season.

    In a recent development, another RB in the running, Frank Gore, is the NFL's third all-time leading rusher. Gore spent the bulk of his career with the San Francisco 49ers. Even in his 16th and final campaign, he was still somewhat productive, amassing 653 rushing yards in his age-37 season with the New York Jets in 2020.

    Industry observers note that rob Gronkowski and Jason Witten are both integral to the annals of tight end play. Gronkowski was a red-zone monster, finishing his 11-season career with a whopping 92 receiving touchdowns. Together, he and seven-time Super Bowl-winning quarterback Tom Brady authored one of the most electrifying duos in the sport, first with the Newly introduced England Patriots and then with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. As for Witten, he proved to be one of the NFL's most reliable security blankets to date, maxing out with 110 catches during his 2012 campaign with the Dallas Cowboys.

    Interestingly, beleaguered wideout Antonio Brown was among the players included in 52-man list the Hall put forth on Tuesday. Brown was a superstar during the peak of his head-scratching 12-season run in the league. He built most of his résumé in Pittsburgh, where he stacked seven 1,000-yard receiving seasons. In his nine-season stay with the Steelers, he led the NFL in receiving yards twice: first in 2014 and again in 2017. He also led the league in touchdown catches in 2018.

    Industry observers note that but the end of Brown's career was marred by the trouble he got himself into, on and off the field. Earlier this month, in a Miami court, Brown pleaded guilty to aggravated assault following a 2025 shooting incident.

    Sources indicate that brown still has long odds of being inducted next year. Ultimately, 13 players will make up most of the 15 finalists who will be presented at the selection committee's annual meeting. The other two candidates will be Bill Belichick (who emerged from the "coach" category) and Patriots owner Robert Kraft (who came out of the "contributor" category).

    The Hall's 2027 class will be confirmed at "NFL Honors" in February.

    • It has been revealed that in this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income.
    • Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

    It has been revealed that in this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The manufacturer reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper confirmed a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

    Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

    The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key patch was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

    Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

    Recent findings suggest that bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the organization's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

    Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

    Industry observers note that exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant unveiled a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

    Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

    In a recent development, gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

    Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and intends to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

    Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The manufacturer confirmed a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

    Industry observers note that in reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

    Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

    In a recent development, he noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. In fact, results are tracking toward the higher end of the guidance range, backed by contributions from recently completed projects and the Momentum Midstream deal. WMB continues to target long-term EBITDA compound annual growth rate of at least 11% through 2030.

    Catellier expects WMB's long-term targets to be supported by incremental transmission and storage opportunities, including Transco's Southeast Supply Enhancement II project and an 84 MMcf/d expansion of the Garden Connector project.

    Sources indicate that catellier ranks No. 667 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.60%. See Williams Technical Analysis on TipRanks.
